transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-22 15:00 UTC — Duration 52m — Recording id fb-20261222-cobaltgen-01
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (CobaltGen Lead Infra), Tomás Alvarez (Platform Eng), Ruth Chen (Security), Ethan Li (SRE)

Auto Summary: Quick POC scoping to align on residency fence (regions), connectivity method (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), egress/egress-logging constraints, bench plan (latency/throughput targets), and timeline for a 3-week pilot kickoff early January. Key success criteria discussed: 95th percentile latency < 250ms for chat-like workloads at target concurrency, ability to keep all egress in permitted regions with no public internet egress, and verifiable audit logs/KMS integration.

Topics: Success criteria; Workload sizing; VPC peering vs PrivateLink tradeoffs; Region lock and egress constraints; Benchmark plan and tooling; Timeline and next steps.

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone thanks for making time, uh quick intro — i'm lena from redwood inference, this is diego our se. priya, do you want to kick off with what you want out of this call?
[00:12] Priya: yeah thanks. the big thing for cobaltgen is data never leaves our approved regions or our managed accounts. so we need to agree on a residency fence, and then the connectivity — we're evaluating peering vs private link for the pilot. also need a sense of perf — can your hosted endpoints meet our 95th percentile latency targets at our expected qps?
[00:28] Diego: cool, that's helpful. quick clarifying q: when you say approved regions, are we talking a strict region whitelist (e.g. only us-east-1 and eu-west-1) or must we test regional lockdown per account and deny cross-region routes?
[00:42] Tomás: strict whitelist. we operate in us-east-1 for dev and eu-west-1 for prod, we cannot have failover to other regions without a change request.
[00:52] Ruth: and from security perspective, no egress to public IPs for model inputs/outputs, audit logs must be exportable to our SIEM via a private connection, also KMS for key management is required.
[01:06] Lena: makes sense. high level: Redwood supports both VPC peering and PrivateLink patterns for Private deployments. peering gives lower latency and simpler routing but requires route management and cross-account peering; PrivateLink provides finer isolation (ENIs) but can add NAT-like egress behavior depending on your architecture. there are also tradeoffs around cross-region — PrivateLink is regional so you'd need endpoints per region.
[01:38] Diego: i'd add that for the pilot we usually recommend testing both if teams need to evaluate latency vs ops simplicity. Diego: for example, peering in us-east-1 gave one customer ~20ms lower median latency in our internal benches compared to privatelink, but privatelink reduced blast radius and is easier for customers who don't want cross-account routing changes.
[01:58] Ethan: do you support VPC peering with transitive peering blocked? we have some strict hub-and-spoke rules.
[02:06] Diego: yes, transitive is blocked by default. peering will be single-account-to-redwood-account; we can work within your hub-spoke by requesting direct peering into the spoke.
[02:14] Priya: on egress, our requirement is zero public egress: all artifacts, logs, and any S3 calls must traverse either private endpoints or be routed through our NAT/proxy that is in the allowed accounts. can redwood's private deployment honor that?
[02:28] Lena: short answer: yes. we can route egress to your NAT/EGRESS IPs and support endpoint policies; we'll need the CIDR ranges and IPs up front so the runtime can be configured to only talk to those endpoints. Diego will follow up on config details.
[02:40] Tomás: ok great. regarding success criteria — we want throughput sizing guidance. our expected baseline is 50 concurrent chat sessions, average 120 tokens per response, peak concurrency 200 sessions during bursts. what does that map to in qps/tokens per second?
[02:56] Diego: rough calc: 50 concurrent * say 1 request every 6s = ~8 QPS baseline; with 120 tokens per response at token throughput ~ 100 tokens/s per GPU depending on model & quantization. for planning let's capture end-to-end tokens/s. for your peak 200 sessions, that could be 33 qps and ~4k tokens/s. but we'll produce a more accurate sizing once we know the model family, context lengths, and KV cache hit rates.
[03:24] Priya: model family — for pilot we plan to test an open LLM (redwood-curated Llama-3x-like) and a smaller 7B for cost comparison. can you share perf profiles?
[03:36] Diego: yep we'll attach our model perf sheet — includes mean & p95 token latencies for short vs long contexts and with/without KV caching. for the pilot we'll pin to a single model version and then run a variant with quantized weights to measure unit cost improvement.
[03:48] Ruth: on logging/audit — we need per-request traceability back to our request IDs and redwood must log model version and host region. those logs must be shipable over PrivateLink to our SIEM.
[04:02] Lena: that's standard for private deploys; we can stream audit logs via a private endpoint or S3 in your account. we do require a config step to enable per-token or per-request detail — there's a small perf cost if you want per-token logs.
[04:16] Tomás: benchmark specifics — what are you proposing we measure? p50/p95 latency, throughput, cold-start, throughput under KV hits and misses? and how long does a typical run take?
[04:28] Diego: exactly. typical bench includes: steady-state throughput at target concurrency for 10-15 minutes to warm caches; p50/p95 token latency; cold-start test with empty KV; a long-history test with long contexts; and an egress/traffic test to validate no public egress. runs are usually 30–120 minutes total depending on number of configs. for the pilot we can scope one week of bench runs: day 1 connectivity, day 2 steady-state, day 3 failover and residency tests.
[04:54] Priya: can you run tests from our accounts so the traffic never leaves our perimeter? we need that for controls.
[05:00] Diego: yes — we deploy a small test harness in your account that hits the private endpoints; results are posted to a shared bucket in your account. that'll satisfy the no-public-egress requirement.
[05:10] Ruth: how about verifying region-lock enforcement in failover? we want to make sure automatic fallback doesn't route to other regions.
[05:18] Lena: we can configure routing policies: routing by region with strict deny fallback. for the pilot we'll ensure fallback disabled unless explicitly enabled.
[05:28] Ethan: a question on encryption — we use an HSM-backed KMS. can you accept external KMS or do we need to use redwood-managed keys?
[05:36] Diego: for Private deployments you can bring-your-own-KMS (BYOK) via cross-account grants; SE will put together the exact IAM steps. there are a few SRE steps to ensure keys are accessible from the runtime.
[05:48] Priya: good. about metrics — we need token-level cost estimates and a bill of materials for dedicated capacity if we go that route.
[05:56] Lena: we'll provide a cost model for hosted vs dedicated including estimated GPU-hours and token unit cost per 1M tokens. that'll go into the pilot report.
[06:04] Tomás: sample prompts — we have 3 categories: short chat (10–50 tokens), doc-summarization (2k tokens), and code generation (variable). will these all be benchmarked?
[06:12] Diego: yes we'll make a representative prompt set. warn that for long contexts costs jump and latency behaves differently. we'll include cold KV miss cases.
[06:20] Priya: operationally, who will be our day-to-day contact?
[06:24] Lena: me for project coordination, diego for technical. for security deep questions rachel from security ops can jump in; i've cc'd her on the follow-up email.
[06:32] Ruth: ok thanks. can you clarify the difference in audit surface between peering and privatelink?
[06:38] Diego: privatelink flows over ENIs in your account so you get clearer VPC-flow logs per endpoint, peering shows as cross-account routes and you observe traffic in your route tables; privatelink might make per-connection attribution simpler. both can export logs to your SIEM but the implementation differs. there may be slight extra egress hops in some privatelink patterns.
[06:58] Tomás: any known limitations with multi-region failover for PrivateLink?
[07:02] Diego: private link is regional, so multi-region requires multiple endpoints and an external routing decision to pick region. that is more operationally heavy but matches strict residency. peering can support cross-region peering but you said you don't want that.
[07:12] Priya: ok. timeline check — we're targeting a 3-week pilot: week 0 prep, week 1 connectivity + baseline bench, week 2 tuned bench + security checks, week 3 wrap + report. is that feasible?
[07:24] Lena: feasible on our side; we should aim to kick off first week of january (2027-01-05). major constraints are contractual (PO/SC) and security review — if those move fast we can meet that timeline.
[07:36] Diego: i'll draft the bench scripts this week and share. suggestion: we run peering in us-east-1 for low-latency test and privatelink in eu-west-1 to validate region-by-region patterns.
[07:48] Ethan: what about egress surveillance — can you generate a report that shows all destination IPs and confirm they match our allowed list?
[07:54] Diego: yes the perf harness includes egress reporting from the runtime side and client-side pcap-ish reporting. we'll deliver a CSV of destination IPs/ports and timestamps.
[08:04] Priya: any blockers you foresee?
[08:08] Diego: only missing items are your CIDR ranges, KMS grant policy decisions, and approvals for peering from network ops. once we have those we'll schedule the peering request.
[08:18] Ruth: can you send the security checklist now so i can start the review?
[08:22] Lena: yes will send today — includes SOC2 artifacts, pen test summary, and KMS playbook.
[08:26] Tomás: ok last question — fallback policy: we want explicit fail closed on region mismatch. can you confirm you'll enforce that for pilot?
[08:34] Diego: confirm. we'll set routing policy to deny cross-region fallback.
[08:38] Priya: perfect. recap?
[08:40] Lena: recap: 1) Redwood to share runbook and security docs; 2) Diego to deliver perf harness & sample prompts; 3) CobaltGen to provide region list, CIDR ranges, and KMS requirements; 4) schedule kickoff 2027-01-05 pending approvals. success criteria: p95 latency < 250ms for chat baseline, zero public egress, auditable logs to SIEM, and BYOK KMS support.
[09:10] Tomás: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:14] Ruth: thanks.
[09:16] Lena: appreciate it, we'll follow up with the packet and a calendar invite for the kickoff.

Links mentioned: Redwood security packet (link shared in follow up), internal perf sheet (will be attached), bench harness repo (to be shared).

End of transcript.
